en: The Direct Instruction on Mindfulness of the Buddha through the Jewel-King Samādhi, Volume One, with Preface.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Miaoye of Ningjiang, Siming.
Regarding why the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha is called the "Jewel King": it is because, among all samādhis...
It is the supreme samādhi.
It was first proclaimed at Mount Lu and subsequently spread throughout the world.
Throughout successive dynasties, those who have cultivated the practice of rebirth in the Pure Land have been numerous;
their accounts have been recorded for the world,
and the evidence of their realization is abundant.
From antiquity until the present, it has been richly preserved in written records;
whether Chan or Teaching, there is none that is not revered,
and from the holy to the ordinary, all alike look up to it with admiration.
However, those of shallow capacity in this final age fall ill because of the medicine itself;
they do not seek the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss in the Western Quarter,
but instead seek it within the conceptual shadows of discrimination.
Many fall into this view;
harboring inner pain and grief,
they lament that their efforts have been spent in vain.
Although he practiced without manifest signs of attainment,
he compiled a collection by extracting the profound essentials from various Pure Land sutras and the commentaries and sub-commentaries of the different schools.
Although these words lack literary refinement,
none dared to edit them according to their own whims; rather,
they were intended for self-reflection and have been presented to others for their consideration.
Therefore, by means of the Jewel-King Samādhi, one recollects the Buddha directly, designating his name.

First, regarding the environment and inhabitants of Sukhāvatī: Originally, the World-Honored One, the Holy Lord and Unsurpassed Perfectly All-Knowing One, universally responds to the capacities and needs of sentient beings.
Descending from the Tuṣita Heaven to manifest in the world,
he preached the Dharma in more than three hundred assemblies over forty years,
causing all sentient beings to equally realize the true and eternal.
Finally, at the assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, he preached the Lotus Sūtra,
enabling sentient beings to open, reveal, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
thus was his original intent for appearing in the world fully realized.
However, the path for transcending the world and delivering sentient beings is not unique to Śākyamuni alone;
all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time are without exception like this.
And yet, within the dharma-gates through which Śākyamuni manifested his transformative teachings throughout his single lifetime, [there is a specific teaching].

If one seeks that which, through the resonance of appropriate conditions, gives rise to the profound karmic affinity for Buddhahood—being most simple and easy yet possessing high merit and a swift path—nothing surpasses the single dharma-gate of seeking rebirth in the Pure Land. Indeed, this is the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation.
The primary cause was that in the distant past, during immeasurable kalpas, the Bhikṣu Dharmākara was a great king.
Having heard the Dharma preached by the Buddha Lokeśvararāja,
he subsequently renounced his kingdom, left the household life, and became a bhikṣu.

That Buddha further expounded for him in detail matters such as the adornments of two hundred and ten billion buddha-fields, and the differences between the coarse and the subtle, the good and the evil, among humans and devas.
Having heard this, Dharmākara—
Thereupon, before the Buddha, he made forty-eight kinds of great vows,
vowing that when he attained Buddhahood,

there would be no obstacles in his land— such as the three miserable realms, the three poisons, the eight sufferings, the eight difficulties, the nine afflictions, the ten entanglements, or any other hindrances whatsoever.
Those born in my land all abide in right determination;
they are people who have attained patience, awakened the mind, and achieved liberation through supreme wisdom—
even those who attain birth through as few as ten recitations.
If it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
At that time, the great earth shook violently.
Heavenly flowers rained down,
celestial music resounded spontaneously,
and the Buddha bestowed upon him a prophecy.
Now he has already attained the fruit;
ten kalpas have passed since he became a Buddha,
due to the excellence of his former vows.
His merit, supernormal powers, radiance, strength, fearlessness, and so forth surpass those of the Buddhas of the ten directions;
his name is Amitābha. This is the land where that Buddha Amitābha dwells.
From this Sahā world, proceeding directly to the west, passing through one hundred trillion lands,
there is a land named Sukhāvatī,
or alternatively, Anurakṣa.
He is currently residing there,
and by virtue of his former great vows and supernatural powers,
he expounds the Dharma to gather in those sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions who practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
Sentient beings who are born [into this state] attain non-retrogression;
even their moments cannot be fully counted,
let alone those who liberate others throughout successive kalpas.
There is no limit to those who are born there;
it exceeds even what could be expressed by fine motes of dust or the sands of the Ganges.
That Buddha-land is adorned with such supreme excellence that it surpasses all throughout the ten directions.
There are various jeweled ponds;
according to their size, they are all composed of the seven treasures.
There are also some large ponds.
Its dimensions were vast and expansive;
he dwelt precisely in its center,
where the bottom was strewn with golden sand.
Along the edges were laid out walkways and staircases.
Above the ponds stood further multi-storied pavilions,
rising in thousands of tiers and ten-thousands of layers, vast and exquisitely beautiful.
Its radiant brilliance is beyond full description.
Within that pond, the water of eight virtues— fragrant, delicious, pure, and transparent— overflows and fills it to the brim,
consisting of fourteen qualities.
Within all those immeasurable ornaments,
sounds flow upward and downward,
proclaiming and expounding immeasurable Dharma gates.
Within this wondrous water, there are further sixty billion lotus flowers made of the seven precious gems,
perfectly round and symmetrical.
Water flows between their petals, possessing four colors and four radiances.
The ranks and grades of the three classes are arranged in orderly succession;
their fragrant purity and subtle excellence outshine that land.
The jeweled ground is level and even, accomplished through the power of aspiration.
Upon that ground, there are further sevenfold railings and sevenfold rows of trees;
jeweled banners, pavilions, canopies, and pearl tassels are each infinite, extraordinary, and exquisitely beautiful.
All around, it was arrayed with magnificent adornments throughout that land.
Furthermore, in the void,
there were celestial garments, celestial incense, celestial flowers, celestial silks, and celestial music.
Each was immeasurable;
they were scattered and diffused in profusion throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space.
Such were the immeasurable articles of adornment.

All were composed of inconceivable multitudes of precious jewels, such as gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, *vaidūrya*, *cintāmaṇi*, and *aśmagarbha* diamond-mani wish-fulfilling jewel kings.
Within each of these various jewels, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of jewel-colored light-kings are emitted,
mutually reflecting and illuminating one another, each shining throughout the entire trichiliocosm.
Their radiance interlaces without mutual obstruction,
reaching the very limits of space and being inexhaustible;
thus, each of these infinite lights and each of these adornments is likewise.
In the midst of the void, there were celestial music, fragrant flowers, rare birds, and nets of bells; their sounds were elegant and correct,
the registers and notes pure and penetrating,
resonating with a rhythmic clarity.
It emits immeasurable and boundless subtle sounds;
these sounds pervade everywhere,
without interval or interruption.
They are able to expound upon suffering, emptiness, non-self, and the various pāramitās;
they extol the path to bodhi and praise the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha;
or they speak of the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, and the path.
The practices of all bodhisattvas:
the truths, the objects of focus, the perfections, the powers,
the fearlessnesses, and so forth.
The eighteen unique qualities;
great kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity;
and inconceivable, immeasurable Dharma gates.

The Dharma he preached was that the material and spiritual worlds, as well as the primary and secondary elements, throughout the three periods of time and the ten directions, are interpenetrating and unimpeded;
and he exhorted them to diligent effort.
It is no different from the voice of the Buddha.
When the sentient beings of that land hear this Dharma, they all,
in every thought-moment, follow according to their inclinations.
They will swiftly be able to realize and enter the immeasurable liberations, all the factors of enlightenment, and the superior practices of the three vehicles,
attaining them without distinction from what they have heard from the Buddha.
Even though they are ordinary beings,
by hearing this Dharma, they naturally apply themselves with diligence,
such that not even a single thought of weariness arises.
How could there be any further falling back?
Furthermore, that land consists solely of men and has no women;
they are born by transformation from lotus flowers and do not dwell within a womb.
Exquisite garments and delicious flavors can bring about the joy of the Dharma;
whatever one desires arrives entirely according to one's thoughts.
There is no cold or heat, no day or night;
there is no birth, old age, sickness, or death;
there are no earth, stones, or mountains.
There were no three evil paths of rebirth;
they traveled through the void and walked beneath the trees.
When he wishes to perform buddha-work and manifest supernormal powers,
all proceed from his mental intention;
furthermore, his lifespan is infinite.
Thus, its various forms of bliss are boundless;
hence it is named "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī).
How much more so, then, are the merits, radiance, majestic spiritual power, and marks and signs of the World-Honored Amitābha, each numbering eighty-four thousand!
Like Mount Meru, he sat upon a great lotus lion-throne,
its magnificent adornments outshining even the void of space.
The great ocean cannot equal Mount Meru;
the merit of the white tuft between his eyebrows is even more sublime,
like the sun spreading its radiance so that all other lights are eclipsed.
Within the light, emanated Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Śrāvakas each radiate light that shines afar across dust-mote lands to gather in and sustain sentient beings;
those two Great Beings do likewise.
Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and all the great bodhisattvas of vast conduct reside in that land.
Those who are in their final birth before Buddhahood are exceedingly numerous;
all these supreme virtuous beings assemble together in one place.
May they all become virtuous friends;
taking the Buddha as their teacher,
may they draw near to his compassionate countenance.
Upon hearing the primary truth (*paramārtha*),
one transcends the three realms instantaneously and realizes non-arising (*anutpāda*).
One soars far above the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and brings the two types of awakening (*bodhi*) to perfection.
How much more so, then, could one, in every thought-moment, make offerings to the Triple Gem of the ten directions,
accomplish all dharma-gates,
sport with supernormal powers, and purify buddha-lands?
He even enters the three miserable realms and the six paths of rebirth;
he radiates light to shatter darkness and rescue suffering sentient beings,
or again, he manifests emanations throughout every atom and land.
Guiding according to circumstances and dispensing medicine according to the ailment,
just like the Buddha’s vast compassion.
In every thought-moment,
may they fulfill all the practices and vows of Samantabhadra and possess the wisdom of Mañjuśrī.
Possessing great power like Avalokiteśvara,
they shall equally realize Bodhi.
Abiding in the same state as the Buddha,
even though the natures of all sentient beings are obscure and dull,
they are able to hear this teaching.
Who would not rejoice and give rise to faith and delight? Yet,
although that wondrous land and its adornments exist within my own mind,
[I do not yet perceive them].
If it were not for the fact that the Tathāgata Amitābha, in past lives, practiced the bodhisattva path for the sake of delivering sentient beings in incalculable numbers,
how could he have achieved this?
One should know that the adornments of that Buddha’s practices and vows are boundless and inexhaustible.
Therefore, the Tathāgata dwells in that land; this precious realm,
in which his great vows are fulfilled, has been perfected,
with both the primary and secondary adornments fully complete.
Regarding such adorned environments and their inhabitants,
even if bodhisattvas and śrāvakas— numbering as many as the atoms in a hundred Ganges-sands of buddha-fields in each of the ten directions—
were to praise them with great eloquence according to reality, [they could not exhaustively describe them].
It shall continue until the end of the future, being inexhaustible.
If sons or daughters of good family hear such an exposition as this, [they will attain great merit].
Those who, with a sincere heart, believe and rejoice in desiring to be born in that land,
should act according to the Buddha’s teaching and fully give rise to the three minds.
Fully endowed with all the precepts and not transgressing the rules of dignified conduct,
one then proceeds directly with a straightforward mind.
He contemplates that land’s infinite adornments of both the environment and its inhabitants,
as well as the Tathāgata’s pure body, which possesses eighty thousand marks and signs and radiates the light of merit.
Alternatively, one may focus on a single mark or a single object, even as far as the light from the white tuft of hair between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows,
remaining free from falsehood for one thought-moment up to ten thought-moments.
Whether it takes one day or up to seven days—
just as a strong man might take to bend and extend his arm—
one will immediately attain rebirth there.
If there are those with upright faith who recognize that such a land exists and that such a Tathāgata possesses the power of vows and majestic spiritual authority,
and who do not give rise to doubt or confusion,
but are able to single-mindedly and without distraction uphold his name—
One will be born there even without waiting for the fulfillment of one's expected time;
why wait until the retribution of a physical body is complete before being born?
One should know that Amitābha Buddha receives and leads sentient beings [to his land].
Causing them to leave the ocean of suffering and surpassing their own kind parents,
he had already established a great vow in previous kalpas:
there is no suffering that he would not endure.
There is no practice that does not reach its goal;
there is no vow that does not stand firm;
there is no Dharma that is not taught.
For the sake of delivering me, you have employed hundreds of thousands of skillful means;
now is precisely the right time.
Your eyes do not blink.
With arms hanging down, he waited for me;
ten kalpas have already passed,
and he has not forsaken this thought for a single moment.
It is more painful than having one's heart torn out;
even so, their resolve is so fervent that they enter into the cycle of birth and death.
I have traversed the three realms of existence;
I did not shrink from the toil of the fierce fires of hell.
If I were to turn my mind toward the Buddha, [I would do so now].
Like a child longing for its mother,
when one’s heart is truly comforted,
one will attain rebirth without exceeding the present moment of mindfulness.
Why must one necessarily wait for the duration of ten recitations before attaining rebirth? 2.
Refuting the False and Revealing the True. Second: A practitioner who wishes to be born in that land and escape birth-and-death [must understand this].
First, one must deeply discern the true and false aspects of the mind that seeks rebirth in that land.
Specifically, one should consider whether such a world of Ultimate Bliss exists as an external object or as something within the mind.
If it resides in the mind,
there is only empty conceptualization;
there is no land that can be produced.
If one remains within the sensory objects,
although there is a place of birth,
one will again lose the mind.
If you claim that both mind and object are sought after simultaneously,
then since my body and mind are one,
how could they possibly arise in two places?
If one were to claim that the mind and its objects are one and that each moment of mind seeks its object,
then from this point forward, the mind and its objects remain distinct;
it is difficult to say they are one.
Furthermore, the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss and the Sahā world differ in their purity and defilement;
moreover, the World-Honored One has bestowed his teachings,
commanding that one abandon the defiled and seek the pure.
How can a single meaning be attained?
Since the four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) cannot be sought,
some may say that every place is the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Some say that the purity of mind is itself the Land of Ultimate Bliss;
others say that the Land of Ultimate Bliss is not separate from this very place.
If one interprets it in this way:
All such views are termed wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
Yet, for these reasons, I cannot remain silent.
If they were to claim that the Pure Land resides within the mind...
Even if you falsely recognize this mind as dwelling within my present body,
since it is within the body,
it can only be called "seeking the mind."
What is meant by "seeking birth"?
Could it be that our World-Honored One did not know that the Land of Ultimate Bliss resides within the mind,
yet spoke of it as being beyond ten trillion lands to the west?
Furthermore, how could it be that one is unable to point to and describe the internal mind,
yet is only able to speak of external objects?
Now, Amitābha Buddha is currently preaching the Dharma in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.
The actual reality is manifest before us;
these are the sincere words of the Sages—
how could one dare not to believe them?
Yet one does not know that this mind of conditioned images, which is outside [the self], is in fact the True Mind of the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
This True Mind of mine is like that great ocean—neither increasing nor decreasing.
Yet you falsely claim it to be an external object.
You say that the Pure Land exists within the mind of reflected images;
this mind of reflected images is like a single bubble upon the ocean.
Arising and ceasing are entirely delusive,
yet you falsely claim them to be the mind.
If you stubbornly cling to this false view, [you will remain lost].
If you do not believe that there is a Pure Land outside,
but instead believe it exists within your mind of reflected images,
then that mind of reflected images has no substance.
One cannot seek birth within the mind by means of the mind;
yet one does not realize that although that Land of Ultimate Bliss is in the west,
the western direction is none other than my own true mind.
The true mind has no inherent nature;
it reveals my own mind through those names and essences.
Yet, these names and essences are fundamentally empty.
This is precisely my own mind manifesting its form;
mind and objects are of one substance, and living beings and Buddhas share the same source.
Seek that Buddha.
One should immediately seek one's own mind;
it is not sought externally.
One must investigate one's own mind.
One must seek that Buddha;
how could one be deluded by anything else?
In this way, there is grasping and rejecting, and joy and aversion.
Blazing with attachment to signs,
they follow whatever I seek;
how could they ever turn their minds outward?
Because the mind is capable of encompassing all,
one knows that this mind perfectly envelops all environments and beings— down to their physical forms and mental states,
as well as their purity and defilement.
The causes and effects of the Buddhas' birth,
and all phenomena of the three periods and ten directions,
are fully encompassed within it without exception.
They share the same experience; yet,
when seeking a single external characteristic,
it is utterly unfindable.
Although there are no external forms,
though undivided it is divided;
purity and defilement appear distinct.
Therefore, one should seek in this manner;
how could one possibly seek it within the deluded mind? One should make such an aspiration and seek it thus.
This is what the Buddha has certified.
It is for those in the world who do not recognize their own fundamental mind,
who are foolish and lacking in wisdom.
One does not seek the Buddha of Western Sukhāvatī,
but seeks instead within one's own physical heart— the illusory mind of conditioned reflections—
claiming that this is the Pure Land of Mind-Only and the original nature of Amitābha.
Truly, they are far apart.
Yet that Land of Ultimate Bliss does not depend on the illusory mind of reflected images;
furthermore, the form-body of Amitābha does not reside within the physical aggregates of sentient beings.
If you seek the Buddha who is your own original nature within the mind and heart of this present body, which is a shadow-like reflection conditioned by the four great elements,
do not seek the Buddha of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Then the deluded mind would arise and cease,
and the Buddha would likewise arise and cease. Because the Buddha would arise and cease, [the Dharma would not be eternal].
Samādhi will not be accomplished.
Even if one seeks it and attains something,
one will merely become a Buddha of birth and extinction.
Returning to the land of birth and death,
one does not accomplish right practice.
As the Sūtra says:
By means of the samsaric mind,
one gives rise to samsaric views; thus,
that nature of perfect enlightenment likewise undergoes cyclic revolution.
This is precisely that meaning.
If one wishes to leave behind all deluded views and be born directly there,
one need only seek Amitābha Buddha in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, beyond ten trillion lands to the west.
By means of the wondrous contemplation that accords with the nature of reality, one contemplates it as it truly is,
causing the marks and signs of the Tathāgata’s original enlightenment to manifest therein.
When this merges with the true mind of the initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*) of myself and all sentient beings,
it is revealed herein that the initial and the fundamental are in mutual accord.
Sentient beings and Buddhas mutually respond;
thus samādhi is perfected,
and right practice is established.
Only in the realm of non-arising and non-ceasing can one truly be born.
Thus, we know that this mind pervades all places;
it is not even heard of in the hells.
Not only in Sukhāvatī;
even regarding the suffering places of the hells, one now seeks to depart from them in accordance with one's nature,
and regarding the nine grades of Sukhāvatī, one now seeks to be born there in accordance with one's nature.
Relying solely upon the teachings of the sūtras and following the melodic voice of the Buddha’s Dharma,
one seeks to leave suffering behind and attain happiness, proceeding from the state of an ordinary person into that of a sage.
In truth, it does not exist outside of one's own mind-nature;
therefore, it is called the Pure Land of Mind-Only and the Original Nature Amitābha.
This does not mean that one seeks it from within a deluded mind.
The deluded mind has no substance;

how, then, can it be called the Buddha who is the very nature of the Mind-only? Those who seek [the Buddha] within their own deluded minds of conditioned reflections— [Note: The original Chinese sentence appears to be incomplete, as it ends with "者" (those who). The translation reflects this structural incompleteness.]
To take the physical body, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth, as well as the oceans of lands throughout the ten directions,
as external objects; yet to seek these within one's own unmoving true mind,
is to regard the oceans of lands throughout the ten directions, the great earth, the mountains, and the rivers as the internal mind.
If one knows that the ocean of lands in the ten directions is identical to the internal mind,
they are integrated into a single whole; therefore,
I may, according to my own will, abandon the defiled and take up the pure within it.
To loathe the east and rejoice in the west is nothing other than one's own mind,
for it is because that Buddha of the great vow’s fruition truly exists and is able to draw one in.
Therefore, there is nothing one seeks that cannot be attained.
If one were to claim that the ocean of lands in the ten directions constitutes external objects,
then one would be splitting reality into two separate fragments.
Therefore, the moment a thought stirs, one immediately deviates from the essence of the Dharma and loses its function,
failing to attain one's own mind.
Because this nature-only possesses the causal Buddha but lacks power and function,
although one seeks it, nothing is obtained.
Furthermore, the deluded mind is merely a false reflection produced by conditions.
Delusion exists within the physical body;
there is no land from which it can arise.
The true mind contains and nurtures all lands and dust-motes.
The environment and inhabitants of Ultimate Bliss are inherently complete;
if one seeks them, one will certainly be born there.
When the deluded mind abandons the external and turns toward the internal, [rebirth occurs].
The true mind takes what is external as internal,
because there is no external apart from the internal.
Thus, one seeks externally for a Buddha characterized by form.
One then seeks one's own mind;
because it is not real internally,
seeking within, one finds no substance— only a reflected image.
When one does not perceive one's own mind,
the deluded mind and its objects appear vividly;
yet when the true mind is realized, mind and object are one and the same.
The deluded mind arises and ceases without basis;
the true mind is unmoving and unshakable.
The deluded mind exists in the cause but lacks the fruit.
From beginning to end there is arising and ceasing;
the true mind’s cause and effect are consistent,
and its nature and cultivation mutually penetrate one another.
Thus we know that when seeking from the true mind and the deluded mind,
the difference between them is such;
in terms of time, it is no less than the disparity between a day and a kalpa.
If one discusses their locations, they are not merely as vastly different as heaven and earth;
yet if one discusses the reality of their essence, the Perfect [Mind] envelops the ten voids,
while delusion resides within the body.
If one employs the truth, one cuts across the Sahā world horizontally and emerges directly from birth and death;
if one employs the false, it is like boiling sand to make rice.
It takes kalpas to achieve [enlightenment] through such means.
Therefore, practitioners who resolve to attain Bodhicitta and seek rebirth in a Pure Land—
how could they possibly seek only their own conditioned shadows and deluded minds?
To not seek the true Buddha of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is truly lamentable;
it is like desiring to go west while facing east.
It is like wishing to ascend while embracing a stone;
seeking fire from water,
or looking for water within fire.
How could it be attained? Alas!
People of today do not recognize that the true mind pervades all places;
they fail to see the essence revealed within form itself.
Yet they falsely identify the reflected images of conditioned objects as their fundamental nature;
how extremely erroneous this is!
For example, it is like a person who mistakes a thief for their own son;
their family's wealth and treasures will surely be consumed and destroyed.
It is likewise with the false conceptualization of reflected images as being the mind;
if this consciousness-seed were a thief, [it would be so].
The thief does no harm;
knowing that the mind is illusory,
how could even illusion cause injury?
However, one must not recognize those [images] as being the actual environment and inhabitants of Sukhāvatī.
This is why the Great Master Fǎzhì of Sìmíng spoke of "pointing to the delusory as being itself the True" and discussed the "contemplation of the Buddha and the contemplation of the mind."
I have never at any time repudiated the reality of the Pure Land’s environment and its inhabitants;
yet alas, in later generations, false views arose like swarms of bees and demonic factions blazed like fire.
They destroy the Buddha-dharma and sever the lineage of the Buddhas,
falsely imagining that the wondrous land of Sukhāvatī exists within the mental reflections of their own conditioned perceptions.
Yet they are unwilling to seek it in the West;
how utterly perverse this is!
Those common folk of the streets have not even heard the correct teaching.
Those who secretly transmit such false views and thereby mislead others may yet be excused, even though they cannot escape the retribution of suffering in hell.
Yet those among the fourfold assembly who have left home, wearing the shaven heads and square-cut robes, share this same view;
they are all the more pitiable.
If they were truly seeking liberation from birth and death, [they would not be so].
One will certainly regard this teaching as correct. However,
if there are those whose obstructions are heavy who cannot accord with this Dharma-gate, [they shall not be blamed].
Then you should further examine how the objects of this deluded mind that perceives reflections arise;
since this false mind has no substantial essence,
it merely follows my own arising and ceasing.
Consequently, he falsely claims it is his "self.
Because he falsely identifies with this self,
he asserts that this mind dwells within his current physical body.
That is to say, this physical body dwells within the present world;
that is to say, this world in turn dwells within the present space.
This nature of space is vast and immeasurable.
Universally relinquishing all dusty lands,
one thus makes the great realm empty and small;
the mind becomes inferior to the body.
A single thought-moment is so subtle that it cannot be pointed out or displayed;
how could one possibly [rely upon] this most minute and peripheral deluded mind, which lacks any substantial essence in even a single thought-moment?
Yet one seeks therein the wondrous realm of the Pure Land’s environment and its inhabitants.
To seek what cannot be sought—
how utterly deluded this is!
Once this meaning is understood,
one knows that such emptiness is boundless and,
though it cannot be measured, [is nonetheless realized].
Originally, they did not emerge from my Great Awakened Pure Mind,
just as a stray cloud appears within the vast clarity of the sky;
how much more so, then, do all worlds exist within space?
How much more so this physical body within the world?
How much more so this deluded mind within the physical body?
Thus, one knows that the deluded mind is subtly attached.
The realms are vast, empty, and perfect;
from the minute to the immense,
nothing exists outside the compass of my present fundamental mind.
Therefore, know that my mind is like space,
while that space is like dust.
My mind is vast, boundless, and bottomless.
Encompassing the empty space, atoms, lands, and all sentient beings throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, it surrounds their physical bodies and deluded thoughts;
yet they seek to find even a single dharma existing outside of the mind.
It is utterly ungraspable.

although it is a single mind, [it is so].

One should realize that the Pure Land is mind-only and practice accordingly;

One may exclusively maintain a single mantra,

even to the point of burning incense and scattering flowers.
Perform repentance during the six periods of the day;
completely cast aside worldly entanglements and focus the mind with single-minded concentration.

Because profound cultivation is itself non-cultivation;

Therefore, I now prostrate and exhort you, sons of the Buddha:
